sentences.text: Eotriceratops was a large, herbivorous dinosaur belonging to the family Ceratopsidae and the broader class Ornithischia.
It is classified within the subfamily Chasmosaurinae and the tribe Triceratopsini, placing it among the horned dinosaurs with elaborate frills.
The holotype skull was estimated to be around 3 meters long, featuring a short frill compared to some relatives.
Its maxilla, or upper jaw bone, bore at least thirty-five tooth positions, while the squamosal bone displayed at least five episquamosals.
Forward-curving eye horns, estimated at 80 centimeters in length, projected from the sides of the skull.
This massive animal measured between 8.5 and 9 meters in length, with some estimates reaching up to 12 meters.
Fossil evidence reveals three bite marks above the eye, interpreted as traces of scavenging behavior where another animal attacked the skull.
Eotriceratops is very similar to Triceratops but is 2 million years older, more primitive, and also large in size.
Barnum Brown discovered the skeleton in August 1910 in southern Alberta, Canada, but he neglected it at the time.
The fossils were found at Dry Island Buffalo Jump Provincial Park, between coal seams, leading to the species name xerinsularis, meaning "of the dry island."
The holotype specimen, cataloged as RTMP 2002.57.5, consists of a partial skeleton with a skull but lacks the lower jaws.
The genus Eotriceratops was formally named and described by Xiao-Chun Wu, Donald B. Brinkman, David A. Eberth, and Dennis R. Braman in 2007.
As a herbivore, Eotriceratops likely faced threats from predators, evidenced by bite marks on the eye area near the base of the left horn.
These marks are interpreted as evidence of scavenging behavior, suggesting the animal may have been attacked after death or while injured.
Cladistic analysis suggests Eotriceratops was a close relative and sister species to Triceratops, Nedoceratops, and Torosaurus.
Due to its older age, the authors considered Eotriceratops to be more basal, or lower on the evolutionary tree, than Triceratops, Nedoceratops, and Torosaurus.
The holotype specimen lived about 68.8 million years ago during the early Maastrichtian stage, with other dating placing it between 67.6 and 68 million years ago.
Eotriceratops is older than any other Triceratops-group ceratopsid, filling a biostratigraphic gap between the early and late Maastrichtian stages.
Researchers debate whether Eotriceratops is the sister species of Triceratops or a more basal ancestor to it due to its greater age.
In 2010, Gregory S. Paul renamed the species Triceratops xerinsularis, but this classification is not widely accepted by other researchers.
